 Early voting surges across New York as Hochul, Blakeman make final push
 BY 
 Jack Arpey 
 New York State 
 PUBLISHED 7:09 PM ET Oct. 26, 2026 
 PUBLISHED 7:09 PM EDT Oct. 26, 2026 
 SHARE 
 Early voting is underway across New York, with turnout significantly outpacing the 2022 midterm elections as voters prepare to decide who will occupy the governor’s mansion on Eagle street in Albany come the first of the year, and several competitive congressional races.
 More than 485,000 New Yorkers cast ballots during the first two days of early voting, compared to more than 262,000 during the same period four years ago. It’s an increase of approximately 85% in what political experts say is at least an initial leap in enthusiasm as Democrats hope to capture a surge reminiscent of gains made in 2018 and Republicans hope for another polling miss.
 While the state’s early voting totals do not betray party share and shouldn’t yet be seen as an indication of the full total, those experts say there is still information to be gleaned.
 Turnout has increased significantly in counties with competitive congressional races, including Fulton and Essex counties in the 21st Congressional District, where Republican Anthony Constantino faces Democrat Blake Gendebien.
 Substantial increases have also been recorded in places like Rockland and Westchester counties, where Republican Rep. Mike Lawler is defending his seat against Democratic challenger Cait Conley in the 17th Congressional District.
 The numbers are also drawing attention in the race for governor, where Democratic incumbent Kathy Hochul faces Republican Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman.
 Both candidates are making a final push to turn out supporters, particularly in New York City and its suburbs, which could play a decisive role in the outcome.
 Shawn Donahue, a clinical assistant professor of political science at the University at Buffalo, told Spectrum News 1 that turnout in New York City is being watched especially closely in the early days given the importance to Democrats and its role in the unexpectedly close 2022 gubernatorial election.
 “One of the things that we saw in 2022 that helped to make the governor’s race much closer than people had anticipated was that you had really low turnout in New York City,” Donahue said.
 Early voting has increased substantially in the city this year, although the percentage increase has been smaller than in some parts of upstate New York.
 “It seems that there might be more enthusiasm in the Democratic Party for Governor Hochul and some of those voters are coming out to vote in bigger numbers than they were four years ago,” Donahue said.
 Hochul narrowly defeated Republican Lee Zeldin in 2022, a closer-than-expected contest that coincided with Republican victories in several competitive New York congressional districts. Those victories helped the GOP secure control of the U.S. House of Representatives.
 Hochul, who has been campaigning across the state, said she is working to reach voters in every region.
 “I focus on the entire state, and it takes a lot of time and energy but that’s what my job is,” Hochul said this weekend.
 Blakeman, meanwhile, is emphasizing the importance of strong Republican turnout in areas of the city friendly to Republicans, including Staten Island, where he campaigned over the weekend.
 “Here on Staten Island, if we get those record numbers here, we are going to have a sweet victory,” Blakeman said.
 Both candidates appeared at get-out-the-vote events over the weekend and are expected to continue campaigning across the state in the final days before the Nov. 3 election.
